name: Ferrol
title: Ferrol UTM Gauging | Ship Thickness Measurement, Galicia
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Ferrol: bulk carriers at the outer port, offshore wind and heavy-lift vessels, naval-yard region, tank and hull gauging.
h1: Ferrol Ship Thickness Gauging: Outer Port, Bulk Cargo and Offshore Wind Vessels
intro: Ferrol sits at the end of a long, narrow ría in northern Galicia, best known for its naval yard and base, but its commercial port, with an outer harbour on the open coast, handles bulk cargo and increasingly supports offshore wind. Commercial ships calling here are bulk carriers, general cargo and heavy-lift vessels. Our ultrasonic thickness technicians travel from India to the ship, measuring holds, tanks and decks.

highlights.h: Bulk carriers at the outer port
highlights.p: Large dry bulk carriers use the outer harbour for raw materials. Holds become accessible as discharge progresses, which suits frame, hopper tank and bulkhead gauging ahead of survey.
The port is positioned to support offshore wind fabrication and marshalling. Installation and component-carrier vessels take unusual loads, and charterers look for measured hull condition.
Ferrol's shipbuilding tradition means steel fabrication skills nearby. Readings taken at the commercial berths can inform repair work at yards on the Galician coast, in Ferrol or further south.

port.h: The Ría de Ferrol, the outer port and the ships that call
p: Ferrol is reached through one of Galicia's longest and narrowest rías, whose winding approach is overlooked by old coastal forts and leads to a deep, sheltered natural harbour that has served as a naval base for centuries. The Spanish Navy's arsenal and the Navantia shipyard dominate the inner waterfront, and commercial berths are placed apart from that complex. Over recent years the port authority, which also runs the terminals at San Cibrao, has built an outer port on the open coast near the ría mouth, designed to take larger ships than the narrow channel could comfortably admit.

The commercial trade is bulk-led. Raw materials for heavy industry arrive on dry bulk carriers, among them cargoes bound for power generation and metals production, and general cargo ships bring or take steel products and project cargo. The port has also been developed for the offshore wind industry, with its outer harbour and nearby yards set up for the fabrication, marshalling and loading of large structures such as foundations and floating platforms. Heavy-lift ships, component carriers and tugs work with those cargoes, and fishing vessels and small craft use the quays inside the ría.

For gauging, the mix is distinctive. Bulk carriers calling at the outer port bring the standard problems of that ship type: wastage in ballast tanks, frames and hopper boundaries, and abrasion of hold plating. Heavy-lift and offshore-wind vessels have their own: decks and sea-fastening points bear exceptional loads, and charterers ask for evidence of structural condition before accepting a ship for a campaign. The long ría approach and the exposed outer coast mean that weather and pilotage influence timing, so the working plan allows slack for late arrivals and delayed berthing.

Gauging at Ferrol takes place alongside, at the outer port's bulk and general cargo berths and at the commercial quays inside the ría. A bulk carrier discharging at the outer port gives access to the holds as they are emptied, and the sequence of discharge is agreed with the chief officer and the stevedores so the technicians can reach frames, hopper and topside tanks and transverse bulkheads. Decks of heavy-lift and wind component carriers are measured at the quay, with particular attention to sea-fastening areas and the plating around crane pedestals.

The naval yard and arsenal are restricted establishments whose work is not commercial, so merchant ships needing a docking normally go elsewhere on the Galician coast; yards in Vigo have the floating docks and repair quays for most mid-sized ships. Readings taken at Ferrol are formatted as a steel list that goes ahead of the ship to that yard. Where a ship waits at the ría's anchorage, a launch from the agent reaches it, and the sheltered water inside the ría makes boarding easier than on the open coast. Equipment travels with the technicians.
list: Outer port bulk berths — hold frame, hopper tank and ballast tank gauging on large bulk carriers during discharge
Outer port general and project cargo quays — deck and coaming readings on heavy-lift and wind component carriers
Offshore wind marshalling quays — deck, sea-fastening area and ballast tank readings on installation and carrier vessels
Commercial quays inside the ría — hull, tank and deck gauging on general cargo ships and tugs
Fishing and small-craft berths — hull and tank readings on coastal fishing vessels in port
Pre-docking steel lists for yards at Vigo or elsewhere on the Galician coast

context.h: Administration, naval restrictions and the offshore wind build-out
p: Port state control at Ferrol falls under the Paris MoU, carried out by the Spanish maritime administration, the Dirección General de la Marina Mercante, through the local Capitanía Marítima. The commercial port sees a steady stream of bulk carriers of varied age and flag, and the older ones are those inspectors target. The naval base shapes the port in other ways: parts of the ría are restricted to military traffic, and commercial ships follow the pilots' instructions on routing and berthing with that in mind.

EU measures add to the pressure on owners. A ship entering an EU port must hold an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the bloc's recycling legislation, and both the carbon market (2024) and FuelEU Maritime (2025) now apply to shipping. Spain's plans for floating offshore wind have made Galicia's outer ports a focus of public investment, which brings in heavy-lift ships, tugs and installation vessels from across Europe. Charterers on these projects often ask for independent thickness readings before accepting a ship, and the same readings help owners plan maintenance between campaigns.

jobs.p: Most Ferrol work comes from bulk carriers at the outer port and from vessels linked to offshore wind projects. The superintendent or charterer sends the survey status, the vessel's drawings and the compartments of concern, we agree access with the agent and stevedores, and the technicians travel from India once the stay is confirmed. Heavy-lift vessels often have fixed loading schedules, so the plan is built around them. Typical requests include:
list: Hold frame, hopper tank and transverse bulkhead gauging on a Capesize bulk carrier discharging raw materials, ahead of its special survey.
Deck, sea-fastening area and ballast tank gauging on a heavy-lift vessel before an offshore wind component campaign.
Hull and tank readings on a tug used for wind platform towing, to document the structure for the charterer.
Hatch coaming and cargo hold gauging on a general cargo ship loading steel products, in preparation for intermediate survey.
A pre-docking steel list taken on a bulk carrier at the ría anchorage, sent to a yard in Vigo ahead of its dock slot.

logistics: Technicians usually fly to A Coruña's Alvedro airport or to Santiago de Compostela, connecting through Madrid or Lisbon from India, and reach Ferrol by road. The outer port is a further short drive. The ship's agent arranges port passes and any launch for the anchorage, while the naval zones are not part of commercial access. Spain is in the Schengen area, so each technician needs a visa obtained in India, applied for once the ship's stay is confirmed and supported by an invitation naming the vessel. Weather affects arrivals, so travel is booked late.

faqs.q: Can I dock a merchant ship at Ferrol?
faqs.a: The naval yard and arsenal are not commercial repair facilities, so merchant ships usually go to another Galician yard, typically at Vigo. We take readings at Ferrol alongside or at anchor and prepare a steel list that you can send ahead to the yard, so the docking estimate rests on measured plate.

faqs.q: Can bulk carrier holds be gauged during discharge at the outer port?
faqs.a: Yes, as holds are emptied and made safe. We agree a hold-by-hold sequence with the chief officer and stevedores, and measure frames, hopper and topside tank boundaries and bulkheads. Longer discharges allow a systematic programme, while short calls call for a priority list set in advance.

faqs.q: Do you gauge vessels used for offshore wind work?
faqs.a: Yes. Heavy-lift, installation and component-carrier ships take unusual loads, and charterers often want measured evidence of structural condition before a campaign. We gauge decks, sea-fastening areas, ballast tanks and hold structure alongside, and report compartment by compartment for the charterer's vessel acceptance.

faqs.q: Does the naval base restrict commercial gauging?
faqs.a: Parts of the ría are military zones, and commercial ships are directed by the pilots accordingly. Gauging itself takes place at commercial berths and the anchorage, arranged through the ship's agent. The naval yard and arsenal are not part of any commercial gauging programme.
